question: You are playing a game. A \(2 \times 1\) rectangle covers two adjacent squares (oriented either horizontally or vertically) of a \(3 \times 3\) grid of squares, but you are not told which two squares are covered. Your goal is to find at least one square that is covered by the rectangle. A “turn” consists of you guessing a square, after which you are told whether that square is covered by the hidden rectangle. What is the minimum number of turns you need to ensure that at least one of your guessed squares is covered by the rectangle?
solution:
Four possible rectangle positions can be chosen without sharing any squares. This will show why three guesses cannot guarantee success.

Label the grid squares as follows:
\[
\begin{matrix}
1&2&3\\
4&5&6\\
7&8&9
\end{matrix}
\]
Consider the four possible positions covering the pairs
\[
(1,2),\quad(4,5),\quad(7,8),\quad(3,6).
\]
These pairs are disjoint, so each guess touches at most one of them. After any three guesses, at least one pair remains untouched.

This also handles strategies that choose later guesses using earlier replies: follow the first three guesses made when every reply is a miss. A rectangle in an untouched pair would produce exactly those replies. Thus three turns cannot guarantee a hit.

To show that four turns suffice, color squares \(2,4,6,8\) black and the other five squares white. This is a checkerboard coloring, so every horizontal or vertical pair of adjacent squares contains one black square. Guessing all four black squares therefore guarantees a hit.

The minimum is \(\boxed{4}\) turns, choice C.

solutionMethods.explanation:
A guaranteed hit requires the guessed squares to meet every possible rectangle position, so count how many positions three guesses can rule out.

There are \(6\) horizontal positions, since each of the three rows has two adjacent pairs. Similarly, there are \(6\) vertical positions, for \(12\) positions altogether.

For any strategy, consider its first three guesses along the sequence in which every reply is a miss. There are two cases.

If the center is not guessed, each guessed square belongs to at most three rectangle positions. Thus three guesses rule out at most \(3\cdot3=9\) of the \(12\) positions.

If the center is guessed, it rules out the four positions containing the center. Among the remaining eight positions, each other square belongs to at most two: its possible partners are its two neighbors along the outer border. The other two guesses therefore rule out at most four more positions, giving at most \(4+2+2=8\) in total.

In either case, some rectangle position avoids all three guesses, so three turns cannot guarantee success.

Four turns do suffice: guess the middle square on each of the four sides of the grid. Every adjacent pair joins one of these four squares to either a corner or the center, so every rectangle contains one of the guesses.

Therefore the minimum is \(\boxed{4}\) turns, choice C.
